identity.name: NVIDIA CORP
identity.body: NVIDIA is the fabless designer of the accelerated-computing hardware and software on which the AI build-out runs. It designs GPUs and, increasingly, complete systems: the chips, the interconnect that binds thousands of them into one computer, the reference rack designs, and the CUDA software that makes the hardware programmable. The economic engine has shifted almost entirely to the data centre, which now supplies roughly nine-tenths of revenue, with gaming, professional visualisation, and automotive-and-robotics behind it. The defining move is that the unit of sale keeps rising, from chip to board to rack, sold as an integrated AI factory.

classification.body: NVIDIA designs silicon and outsources fabrication, which fixes it at the IP & Design tier rather than the Fabrication tier occupied by its foundry. Its distinctive move is to climb the ladder without leaving that tier: by selling integrated racks, networking, and software it captures value normally booked at the System Integration and Deployment tiers, while remaining, in manufacturing terms, a design house dependent on others' capacity.

bottleneck.headline: A control point at the software and interconnect layer; a dependent at fabrication.
bottleneck.body: The rating answers a narrow question: can customers and rivals route around NVIDIA. The answer splits by layer, and that split is the story. Downstream, two proprietary assets are hard to route around: CUDA, a parallel-computing platform accumulated since 2006 with cross-generation compatibility that protects customers' software investments, and the interconnect (NVLink, InfiniBand, Spectrum-X) that binds thousands of GPUs into one machine. Together they carry an estimated four-fifths or more of merchant AI accelerators. Upstream, NVIDIA owns none of the physical chokepoints beneath it: its most advanced parts are fabricated only by TSMC, packaged with TSMC CoWoS, and fed by a three-supplier memory oligopoly. It sets the terms downstream and takes the terms upstream. That two-sided position is why the rating is HIGH rather than CRITICAL: a near-sole merchant supplier with a deep, contested moat, sitting on chokepoints it does not own.

dependency.control_point: CUDA software and interconnect (NVLink, InfiniBand, Spectrum-X)
dependency.analysis_teaser: Every upstream edge is an oligopoly allocated years in advance, and the fragility is physical, not competitive.
dependency.analysis_body: Why the dependencies concentrate: TSMC holds roughly seventy per cent of global foundry and is the only at-scale source for the leading node near term; CoWoS packaging is effectively sold out, with NVIDIA having pre-booked more than half of projected 2026 capacity; HBM is a three-way race led by SK Hynix, with Micron and Samsung qualified behind it. Downstream concentrates for the opposite reason: CUDA and interconnect lock-in funnel demand back to NVIDIA even as buyers seek alternatives. Where the fragility sits: CoWoS packaging is the binding constraint on how much demand converts to revenue; the same handful of hyperscalers that each represent a tenth or more of revenue are also the most credible competitors, building their own silicon; and the advanced-manufacturing base runs through Taiwan and Korea, a geographic single point of failure. What substitution would cost: upstream there is no near-term at-scale second source, and downstream porting a production workload off CUDA is feasible but costly in engineering time and performance, which is why custom silicon has advanced fastest where a single owner controls the whole stack.

market_context.rank_label: Joint-largest constituent (nine names sit at the cap)

capital.teaser: A cash-generative, net-cash business returning capital primarily through buybacks, with a working-capital signature defined by supply prepayments.
capital.body: Categorical posture, no per-share figures. NVIDIA returns capital primarily through large repurchases, with a fresh multi-tens-of-billions authorisation added in mid-2026 and a small but recently-raised dividend that remains immaterial against free cash flow measured in the tens of billions. The balance-sheet shape that matters for the value-chain thesis is the working-capital commitment to supply: elevated inventory and large prepayments and purchase obligations made to secure scarce TSMC, CoWoS, and HBM capacity years ahead. That is the financial signature of a company converting a supply-constrained input into product, and it is also what turned into charges when China access was withdrawn.

policy.teaser: Two governments pull opposite levers on NVIDIA: it has survived the loss of the China chip market, but the materials and manufacturing risks beneath it remain untested.
policy.body:
Two governments hold levers over NVIDIA's business, and they pull in opposite directions. The United States controls where NVIDIA's chips may be sold. China controls whether the raw materials inside them keep flowing. Neither exposure is unique to NVIDIA. Most companies in the frontier stack face one or the other. NVIDIA is unusual in facing both at full intensity: it is the named target of American chip controls, and, through the systems its processors ship inside, one of the largest consumers of the materials China licenses.

From April 2025 to January 2026, NVIDIA lost its foothold in the Chinese market. In April 2025, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security required a licence to export the H20, the chip NVIDIA had designed specifically to comply with Washington's earlier China restrictions. NVIDIA subsequently wrote off $4.5 billion of H20 inventory and purchase commitments. In July 2025, the Trump administration signalled it would grant the licences after all, a reversal tied publicly to a US-China understanding over rare earths. In August 2025, NVIDIA and AMD reportedly agreed to pay the US government 15% of their China AI-chip revenue as a condition of those licences; the arrangement was reported but never set out in any published rule, and events soon overtook it. Beijing then answered Washington. Through August and September 2025, Chinese authorities discouraged, then reportedly barred, purchases of NVIDIA chips, and NVIDIA halted H20 production. By October 2025, Jensen Huang put it plainly: NVIDIA was 100% out of China, a market that had been roughly a fifth to a quarter of its data-centre revenue. In December 2025, Washington approved sales of the H200, an older chip, to vetted Chinese buyers with a 25% surcharge on the revenue, explicitly excluding the current Blackwell and coming Rubin generations. In January 2026, the Bureau moved to reviewing applications case by case. China ended the episode as a conditional, second-tier market for NVIDIA at best.

The striking part is what the loss did not do. NVIDIA's revenue grew 65% in fiscal 2026, the year the Chinese market closed, and 85% year on year in the quarter that followed. Buyers elsewhere, American cloud companies, Gulf and European governments, took everything China would have bought; the editorial layer describes that demand in full. A market NVIDIA's own leadership sized at up to a quarter of its data-centre revenue closed, and the company's growth did not visibly slow. This is not the same as saying the chip risk is over. The case-by-case review is a valve Washington can tighten at will, NVIDIA's best chips remain banned from China, and the surcharge precedent gives both governments a template for taxing whatever trade resumes. What 2025 proved is narrower: the worst case on the chip side arrived, and NVIDIA's growth survived it.

No such test has been run on the materials side, and that is where the open risk sits. China licenses the export of raw materials NVIDIA's products depend on: the gallium in its power electronics, the germanium in its optics, and the rare-earth elements in the magnets, motors and cooling of the AI systems its chips ship inside. These licences are not one policy but three, and the difference between them decides what happens in November 2026. First, since April 2025, China has required export licences for heavy rare-earth magnet materials. That requirement was never paused and has no end date. Second, in October 2025, China announced two further sets of controls: an expansion of the rare-earth licensing, and new controls on gallium and germanium. Under a one-year US-China truce agreed on 10 November 2025, both were suspended before they took effect. That suspension is what expires. Unless the truce is renewed, the expanded rare-earth licensing resumes on 10 November 2026, and the gallium and germanium controls follow on 27 November 2026. Third, indium, also used in NVIDIA's optics, is controlled under a separate Chinese announcement from early 2025 that was never part of the truce; its licence requirement stands now and does not lapse. What returns in November 2026, then, is the suspended second set. The first and third were never gone.

Whether the truce is renewed is the kind of question NVIDIA spends heavily trying to answer, and the record shows how little that buys. The 2025 chronology above is one reversal after another, licence required, licence granted, market barred, older chip readmitted, and it unfolded despite NVIDIA sharply increasing its Washington lobbying, from around $0.6 million in 2024 to roughly $5 million in 2025. In June 2026 it appointed Bruce Andrews, formerly Intel's government affairs chief and a Commerce Department official under Obama, as its first Chief External Affairs Officer, and it retains prominent Washington lobbying firms including Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, the Vogel Group and BGR Government Affairs. A company with that machinery still could not see the reversals coming. That is the real character of this policy exposure: not a fixed rule NVIDIA can plan around, but a variable that moves faster than even a well-connected company can anticipate.

Why the materials risk outranks the chip risk comes down to substitution. When the chip market closed, NVIDIA found other buyers for the same products; demand moved, the products did not change. A materials stoppage offers no such move. China refines most of the world's gallium and rare earths, the mines and refineries being built elsewhere are years from replacing it, and a licence withheld at the top of the supply chain stops production everywhere below it, regardless of where the final customer sits. The 2025 episode showed NVIDIA can lose a market and keep growing. Whether it can lose a material and keep building is the question November 2026 poses.

Behind both exposures sits a third, so far untouched. NVIDIA's most advanced chips are made and assembled in Taiwan, by TSMC, and the geography layer of this profile maps how much of NVIDIA's supply chain concentrates there and in Korea. The policy point is that this concentration is not only a physical risk but a target: the same instruments both governments used through 2025, licence requirements, export bans, revenue conditions, could be aimed at the Taiwan supply chain directly. Against the loss of a market, NVIDIA has shown it can adapt: China closed, and other buyers replaced it. But if Taiwan's factories stopped, whether by blockade, conflict or policy, there is nowhere else that can make NVIDIA's most advanced chips today, and no past episode shows how the company would cope. The market risk has a proven answer. The manufacturing risk has none.

geographic.teaser: Not a location line but a dependency overlay: revenue is global, production is concentrated in East Asia.
geographic.body: Fabrication and CoWoS packaging in Taiwan, HBM in Korea, substrates in Japan. From the third quarter of fiscal 2026 NVIDIA reports revenue by customer-headquarters location, and the earlier Singapore billing-location line is retired; it notes that end-customer location differs from headquarters, attributing about three-quarters of Data Center revenue from Taiwan-headquartered customers to end customers in the United States and Europe. The load-bearing fact is manufacturing concentration: any disruption to Taiwan, whether geopolitical or physical, would sever the ability to produce the most advanced parts. Diversification is under way but slow.

editorial.notes: The gravitational centre of the frontier stack. NVIDIA's compute silicon enables robotics inference, satellite processing, and autonomous systems. CoWoS packaging capacity is the binding constraint.
editorial.teaser: The four open concerns about NVIDIA, read through the dependency chain.
editorial.body:
There are four open concerns that affect NVIDIA currently. Whether its valuation ran ahead of what AI will ever pay back. Whether its biggest customers, now designing their own chips, will erode its pricing power. Whether the financing behind the AI build-out is circular, with NVIDIA's cash flowing to the same data centres that buy its chips. And whether its supply chain and China exposure are the real limits on its growth. Robotnik does not price companies, so the valuation question stays with the analysts who ask it. The other three run through the dependency chain, and that is where this profile can add something.

Has NVIDIA's lead started to slip? The threat may come from NVIDIA's own customers, as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta each now design their own AI chips. These four are hyperscalers, the companies whose vast data centres rent computing to everyone else, and they buy more of NVIDIA's chips than anyone. Their in-house chips already compete with NVIDIA for scarce parts. Every AI processor needs high-bandwidth memory, a specialised form of it made by only three companies: SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron. Their entire 2026 output was reserved in advance by three buyers, NVIDIA, AMD and Google, with Google reserving memory for a chip it designed itself. The hyperscalers do not do this work alone. Broadcom designs most of these in-house chips under contract, Google's among them. Its AI-chip sales grew more than 140% in a single quarter, and its order book for this work stands in the tens of billions of dollars. None of it has dented NVIDIA's results. Data-centre sales grew 92% year on year in the most recent quarter, because demand still outruns everything the industry can supply; the in-house chips add capacity to a starved market rather than displacing NVIDIA's. The thing to watch is the turn: the point where they stop supplementing and start substituting. One fact frames how that contest can end. None of these challengers owns its supply chain. Whoever wins, the chips are fabricated by TSMC, fed by the same three memory makers, and printed on ASML's machines. The challengers and the incumbent compete downstream of the same chain, which is why Robotnik watches the chain rather than the contest.

Will the demand last? A handful of buyers fund most of the AI build-out. No company has more riding on their spending than NVIDIA. Data centres are now roughly 90% of its revenue, so a spending pause that bruises other chipmakers would break NVIDIA's growth. NVIDIA knows this and is diversifying its customer base. Its leadership describes a shift from near-total dependence on the hyperscalers towards a rough half-and-half split with governments and enterprises. Gulf, European and Asian states are funding national AI programmes. Firms such as CoreWeave rent NVIDIA systems to companies that cannot build their own. The product is the same in every case, and that does not matter much. What matters is that more hands are paying for it, because a broader customer base means no single buyer's retreat is fatal. The caveat is that all these buyers are making the same bet, that AI compute pays for itself, so the diversification protects against one customer pulling back, not against the bet itself failing. The only revenue resting on a different bet is automotive, and at $2.3 billion of $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026, it is 1% of the total. NVIDIA, for its part, is investing as if the demand holds. It has signed long-term memory contracts and paid suppliers years in advance. Colette Kress, its finance chief, returned the company to the bond market in 2026, raising $25 billion, its first bond issuance since 2021, for general corporate purposes and to refinance existing debt.

Where does NVIDIA sit in the chain of dependence? Robotnik maps the frontier stack as a chain: who relies on whom, and who could be replaced. Seen through that map, NVIDIA splits in two.

Facing its customers, NVIDIA sets the terms, including for the four building alternatives. They pay while they build because leaving costs years. Their AI software runs on CUDA, NVIDIA's programming platform. Their data centres are wired with NVIDIA's networking. Both would have to be rebuilt. Their deeper moat is the product roadmap. NVIDIA publishes its chips two to three years ahead, Rubin this year, Rubin Ultra in 2027, Feynman in 2028, and the industry invests against the plan. SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron have begun volume production of next-generation memory for Vera Rubin, a chip NVIDIA has not yet shipped, with SK Hynix estimated to hold 60 to 70% of that work. A challenger cannot simply design a better processor. It must persuade the same suppliers to retool around its roadmap instead, and their most profitable lines are already committed to NVIDIA's. That synchronisation is a moat measured in years.

Facing its suppliers, NVIDIA takes the terms, because it has nowhere else to go. It designs chips but makes none. TSMC both fabricates its processors, at a precision no other manufacturer matches today, and packages them, joining processor to memory in a process called CoWoS whose capacity is committed long in advance. SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron have sold their memory production years ahead, so more cannot be had quickly at any price. Further up the chain sit Ibiden, the Japanese firm that leads in the advanced substrates the largest chips are built on, and ASML, whose lithography is unique to it. Does NVIDIA's size win any of this power back? Some. It is among TSMC's largest customers, and TSMC would feel the loss of that volume. But weight is not leverage when there is no alternative. TSMC could reallocate its capacity to Apple or AMD; NVIDIA cannot move its orders anywhere at the leading edge. The dependence runs both ways, and it does not run equally. Jensen Huang appears to have drawn the same conclusion, because he is paying to secure the chain. NVIDIA put $4 billion into its optical suppliers this year, signed long-term memory contracts, and prepaid capacity. That is the investment of a company whose ceiling is set by what it can build.

Politics runs through all of it. The chain above sits in Taiwan, Korea, Japan and the Netherlands. The raw materials beneath it, the gallium in NVIDIA's power electronics and the rare earths in everything that moves, need Chinese export licences, and the truce covering them lapses in November 2026. The precedent worth holding onto is the one that did no damage. When Washington and then Beijing closed China's market to NVIDIA's chips, growth went around the loss. The export risk that binds NVIDIA is not whether its chips can flow into China. It is whether the materials keep flowing out. The full chronology sits in this profile's policy layer; the geography of the chain sits in its geography layer.

What would settle the debate? Four things. The capital-spending guidance of the hyperscalers, which funds everything. The share of their chip budgets going to their own designs, which measures substitution. Whether NVIDIA's packaging and memory allocations turn into shipped systems, which is the supply limit made visible. And whether the materials truce holds past November, which is the political limit made visible.

Robotnik's reading is that the loud contest is the slow one. Customers replacing NVIDIA is a matter of years. A licence decision or a packaging shortfall is a matter of months. NVIDIA is harder to attack than the competition story suggests, and easier to stop than its results suggest, because its weaknesses sit where an income statement does not show them: in the suppliers above it and the politics around them. Watch this company from upstream.
